      and bloody battles.

      playing game that strives to weave together historical Carolingian
      events and the medieval epics into one coherent chronology.

         n Paladin the players take on the role of young Frankish
         squires or knights in the service of one of Charlemagne’s
         powerful vassals. By going on adventures they will acquire
      glory and riches, become lords of their own lands, build castles
      and found their own family. Hopefully, the road to fame will

      idealism. The player characters are knights, with the privileges

      dualisms — brutal reality versus idealism, and elite privilege ver-

        What are Role Playing Games?

   In a role playing game (RPG), a Gamemaster describes an
   imaginary world to the players, who take on the roles of fic-
   tional characters. They tell the Gamemaster what they wish
   their characters to do and the Gamemaster decides — some-
   times aided by dice to resolve certain actions — what finally
   happens. In this way a tale unfolds in which the Player-knights
   are the acting heroes and their Gamemaster is the story
   director.
      The Gamemaster decides what events take place and
   what all non-player characters (NPCs) do. He presents the
   mysteries, obstacles, monsters, challenges, opponents or
   friends who cross the path of the Player-knights. He is not
   their opponent himself, but rather their guide to adventure.
   The role of a Gamemaster is to create a legend of his own by
   presenting a series of scenarios to his players. Together, these
   adventures form a grand story in which the heroic characters’
   destinies find an expression in roleplaying.
      The game is mostly verbal, so all you need is a bit of pa-
   per, pencils, some dice and a thriving imagination.
   If chivalry and courtesy
   Can satisfy substantial wits,
   You’ll like my history. You are
   A gallant, noble, gracious group.
   You’re spirited and courteous,
   Traits never found in coward hearts.
   Come, listen to my song, the praise
   And boast of errant knights of old.

title: Who Is Charlemagne?
leftColumn:
Relation to the

           King Arthur Pendragon Game
       If you have played King Arthur Pendragon (Pendragon
       for short) before, you will find that Paladin plays almost the
       same, though the subject matter is somewhat different. Many
       of the Player-knight goals in Paladin are the same as those of
       Pendragon — fight for your king or for adventure, woo a lady,
       and become the premier knight of the land or a high noble.
         Paladin uses the Pendragon game as it’s basis. Most
       game mechanics are exactly the same between the two games,
       and players should have no problem transitioning from
       Pendragon to Paladin. However, a few changes have been
       made to reflect the differences between Arthurian Romances
       and the Carolingian Epics.
         First, is the conceit that God loves Charlemagne, and
       loves all those that love Charlemagne. Miracles occur through
       a knight’s love for Charlemagne, not through his love of God.
       The Spiritual/Worldly traits have been removed from the
       game, replaced by the Love [Charlemagne] passion.
         Secondly, the passions of Loyalty [Lord] and Hospitality
       have been folded into the Honor passion. It is impossible for
       an Honorable knight to be disloyal to his lord or inhospitable.
       If you defy your lord or abuse your guests, you lose honor. It’s
       as simple as that.
         Thirdly, weapon skills have been consolidated; one and
       two-handed styles have been combined into a single skill
       — for example, both one- and two-handed swords use the
       Sword skill.
         Fourth, the players’ extended family is given a greater
       emphasis in Paladin than in Pendragon. Players are strongly
       encouraged to have their characters come from the same ex-
       tended family, emulating the gestes.
         Fifth, Player-knights age quicker and probably die soon-
       er than their Pendragon counterparts. Ageing rolls occur
       earlier, and are harsher.
         Sixth, statistics become harder to increase after 16,
       rather than 20, requiring the use of bonus points from Glory
       to improve. The points needed to become a Chivalrous,
       Romantic or Pious knight are increased, so it is harder to
       achieve those goals.
        Paladin is a game for knights. It is based on the standards of
      knighthood found in the original literature about Charlemagne
      and the paladins. It is not about magicians, thieves, or scholars.
      In this game, designed for playing the heavily armed and ar-
      mored chevaliers of Carolingian literature, knighthood is com-
      plex enough!
        The game starts in the ‘realistic’ Dark Ages, but as the game
      progresses, so, too, does historical innovation. The Franks evolve
      into the civilization of the later feudal periods, when the epics
      were written. The game crowds the entire Middle Ages into its
      framework, moving the characters through the equivalent of
      centuries of time, allowing you to experience historical devel-
      opments in armor, weapons, castles and customs in a process of
      accelerating change.

    Charlemagne, by the grace of God,
    King of the Franks and Lombards

    and Patrician of the Romans
  C
      harlemagne is sometimes called the Father of Europe.
      This Frankish king and emperor was probably born in
      742 in the Ardennes and definitely died in 814 at his
  palace in Aachen. In 768, at the death of his father, King Pepin
  the Short, he was crowned King of the Franks, together with his
  younger brother, Carloman.
     In his time, Charlemagne was named Karol or Charles.
  Once his fame had grown into mythical proportions, later
  chroniclers made him into “Charles the Great.” In Latin, he was
  known as “Carolus Magnus,” which was transformed into the
  vernacular name by which he is now best known: Charlemagne.
     During the reign of the former royal family, the
  Merovingians, the lands of the Franks were ravaged by unre-
  mitting tumult, brutality, and anarchy until the Carolingians
  took control of matters. The Carolingians take their name from
  Charlemagne’s illustrious grandfather, Charles Martel (“the
  Hammer”), who defeated the Saracens at Poitiers in 732.
     Under the Carolingians, the Franks rapidly became one of
  the dominant peoples in Western Europe. Their reign saw the
  birth of the feudal system. In fact, the first recorded occurrence
  of the word “fief” dates from this period.
     Charlemagne was seen by later authors as an example of a
  strong monarch who restored justice and social order, promot-
  ed science, and relentlessly fought the enemies of Christ. The
  Charlemagne of the legends is protected and guided by the
  God of the Christians, who communicates with the sacred king
  through dreams and visions, and sends his champions aid in the
  form of miracles, angelic visions, prophetic dreams and other di-
  vine messages.
     Note that we use “Charlemagne” rather than Carolus, Karl,
  or Charles throughout the text, even before he is king. This is
  merely to distinguish him from any other Charles in the game.

title: The Literary Sources
leftColumn:
The Literary Sources

      The events and characters presented in Paladin are based on
      the almost one hundred extant Carolingian epics (French: chan-
      sons de geste), a list of which is given in the Bibliography.
        The chansons de geste are medieval narrative poems of
      knighthood, chivalry and crusade. Most were composed in
      French in the 12th and 13th centuries and deal with the military
      feats of Christian heroes battling pagan enemies, or rebellious
      barons fighting each other or their king. The best-known chan-
      son de geste, and earliest known epic poem about Charlemagne,
      is The Song of Roland.
        The original epics were composed by anonymous singers
      called trouvères. These songs were performed all across the coun-
      try before audiences of differing and changing tastes. They were
      recited as a sort of street theatre at markets, or at noble courts
      by travelling singers or residential minstrels sometimes accom-
      panied by musicians.
        The epics are a celebration of the noble heroes of old. Their
      stories are meant to teach the audience feudal, chivalric, roman-
      tic and Christian values, and to entertain an audience who paid
      the singer and his musicians. This explains the humorous and
      satirical elements in some of the epics.
        The earlier works remain anonymous. Though the Song
      of Roland is attributed to a certain Turold, we don’t know who
      he may have been. Some later songs were written by Adenet le
      Roi, Jean Bodel or Bertrand Bar-sur-Aube, who were quite fa-
      mous in their time.
        The epics were written down some centuries after their
      composition, but they kept the imprint of their former oral
      shape. Formally, a chanson de geste is composed of assonanced
      stanzas of variable length called laisses (“verse-blocks”). The an-
      cient word “gesta” generally refers to “exploits” or “deeds of val-
      or,” but can also signify “family” or “lineage.” So the chansons de
      geste are the “songs of exploits” about Carolingian knights and
      their families.
        Initially, the epics dealt only with Charlemagne and his
      peers, but gradually new tales sprang up about secondary char-
      acters, a known hero’s youth and his previous adventures, or his
      ancestors or descendants. Most of these medieval tales of heroes
      and their marvelous deeds are loosely based on historical events
      of the Carolingian period. These may or may not have taken
      place during Charlemagne’s reign itself, but through a phenome-
      non called “epic concentration,” the historic facts relating to one
      or another Carolingian sovereign are all attributed to the most
      famous among them: Charlemagne.

segments.text: The Literary Sources

The events and characters presented in Paladin are based on
      the almost one hundred extant Carolingian epics (French: chan-
      sons de geste), a list of which is given in the Bibliography.
        The chansons de geste are medieval narrative poems of
      knighthood, chivalry and crusade. Most were composed in
      French in the 12th and 13th centuries and deal with the military
      feats of Christian heroes battling pagan enemies, or rebellious
      barons fighting each other or their king. The best-known chan-
      son de geste, and earliest known epic poem about Charlemagne,
      is The Song of Roland.
        The original epics were composed by anonymous singers
      called trouvères. These songs were performed all across the coun-
      try before audiences of differing and changing tastes. They were
      recited as a sort of street theatre at markets, or at noble courts
      by travelling singers or residential minstrels sometimes accom-
      panied by musicians.
        The epics are a celebration of the noble heroes of old. Their
      stories are meant to teach the audience feudal, chivalric, roman-
      tic and Christian values, and to entertain an audience who paid
      the singer and his musicians. This explains the humorous and
      satirical elements in some of the epics.
        The earlier works remain anonymous. Though the Song
      of Roland is attributed to a certain Turold, we don’t know who
      he may have been. Some later songs were written by Adenet le
      Roi, Jean Bodel or Bertrand Bar-sur-Aube, who were quite fa-
      mous in their time.
        The epics were written down some centuries after their
      composition, but they kept the imprint of their former oral
      shape. Formally, a chanson de geste is composed of assonanced
      stanzas of variable length called laisses (“verse-blocks”). The an-
      cient word “gesta” generally refers to “exploits” or “deeds of val-
      or,” but can also signify “family” or “lineage.” So the chansons de
      geste are the “songs of exploits” about Carolingian knights and
      their families.
        Initially, the epics dealt only with Charlemagne and his
      peers, but gradually new tales sprang up about secondary char-
      acters, a known hero’s youth and his previous adventures, or his
      ancestors or descendants. Most of these medieval tales of heroes
      and their marvelous deeds are loosely based on historical events
      of the Carolingian period. These may or may not have taken
      place during Charlemagne’s reign itself, but through a phenome-
      non called “epic concentration,” the historic facts relating to one
      or another Carolingian sovereign are all attributed to the most
      famous among them: Charlemagne.
        In his Song of the Saxons, Jean Bodel distinguish-
      es three subject matters for poets: the Matter of Rome, deal-
      ing with the classical world and its mythology; the Matter of
      Britain, which tells the stories of Arthur and the knights of
      the Round Table; and the Matter of France, which concentrates
      on Charlemagne and his paladins. Within this last branch, the
      poet Bertrand Bar-sur-Aube, in his Girart de Vienne, divides

In order to build up a coherent Charlemagne mythos for
      this book, we have tried to go back to the most ancient originals.
      Most chansons de geste are hard to come by, even at specialized
      University libraries. And apart from the Song of Roland,
      uniform standard versions are almost non-existent. Whenever
      possible, for each epic a so-called “critical version” was used — a
      reconstruction of the hypothetical “original” story based on the
      preserved fragments.
        We’ve tried to be as exhaustive as possible. Only few gestes
      have been left aside, especially when they are contradicting more
      important ones. For more information about the used sources,
      please take a look at Appendix 2: Bibliography at the end of this
      book.
      Epic  Times

     T
         he Paladin game moves quickly through time. The
         objective is to play through 47 game years (767-814),
         covering the entirety of Charlemagne’s reign. Your first
      character will witness the crowning of Charlemagne as King of
      the Franks and the creation of the order of paladins. He, or his
      family, may fight at Roncevaux and participate in other great
      and deadly battles, share in the period of adventures when quest-
      ing and love rule the royal court. Finally, the Player-knights will
      witness the slow decline of the Empire as the order of paladins is
      gradually disbanded.

      to fully explore the depth of the Carolingian era — both real
      and fantastic. Over time, the Player-knights will interact with
      the main characters, participate in some of the main events, and
      hopefully make a few substantial contributions to the legends of
      Charlemagne themselves.

             A Word About the Quotes

       Throughout this book are quotes from the original epics, as
       well as historical documents like Frankish laws, letters, or po-
       ems written by monks.
         A special historic source is the book written by Dhuoda.
       She was the wife of Bertrand of Septimania and the daughter-
       in-law of William of Gellone, one of Charlemagne’s most fa-
       mous paladins. Her work, a substantial text put to parchment
       by a woman, is the only such book to have survived from the
       Carolingian period. It is written as a guide for her son, whom
       she urges to lead his life as a path to Heaven:
       “I send you this little book written down in my name, that you
        may read it for your education, as a kind of mirror.
       From the first line of this little book
       To its last syllable, know that
       All this is written for your salvation.”
         — Dhuoda, “Prologue”

  47 years of Charlemagne’s reign. To represent this fast-forward
  evolution of the Franks, the Paladin chronology is not static.
  Customs change, armor improves, new weapons and better hors-
  es become available, as well as new troop types and fortifications.
  The pace of these changes is such that 11 years of game time ap-
  proximates a century of history, bringing the campaign not just
  through the Carolingian legends, but through the history of the
  entire European Middle Ages.
  The   Players   as  Knights

  K
      nights are noble warriors who serve a lord. They swear
      loyalty, promising to give their lord good counsel and
      military assistance. In return, a lord must protect and
  avenge his knights. A knight’s main characteristics are loyalty,
  honor, courage and fame.
     So if everybody in the game is a knight, what sets them
  apart?
     Each player must determine for himself who his knight
  will be. What is his personality? What are his ambitions, his
  strengths and weaknesses? Which lord does he serve and what
  social position does he hold? What about his family? All these
  things matter greatly, and ultimately define each Player-knight.
  Glory
  The object of the game is to acquire Glory. Everything a knight
  does that is knightly helps to acquire Glory. He gets Glory
  through his family, fighting, chivalrous and religious behavior,
  possessions and riches, and acquiring high social rank. There is
  no greater pride for a player than to see his knight become one
  of the most respected and famous men of their world: a paladin
  of Charlemagne!

  Family

  The game is deadly to Player-knights. Their job is combat, and
  the game is designed to be dangerous. Characters need to be
  careful! Every character is going to retire or die, either through
  violence (quite common) or old age. Mortality makes the game
  more poignant and the characters more affected with the con-
  cerns of real people. But there is a solution to this mortality: a
  family. One of the concerns of every knight is to raise a family, so
  when your character retires from play through death or old age,
  all his possessions go to the next character you play (his heir or
  one of his relatives). The coat of arms, horse, manor and family
  name live on!
     Your knight is more than just an individual, he is a member
  of a great house. The bonds of blood assure a Player-knight that,
  after his demise, his works and ambitions will continue. By ac-
  complishing glorious deeds, a Player-knight increases the honor
  of his family. It gives Player-knights from the same house com-
  mon goals and concerns, stimulating group play.

      passion a knight can obtain nearly superhuman prowess!

        off their horse called themselves a knight.

      The higher and more refined standard of knightly conduct is
      called chivalry. It creates an even larger gap between commoners
      and nobles, turning knights into paragons of virtue and civiliza-
      tion. Chivalrous knights follow not only a more elaborate and
      peaceful code of honor, they also pay their full respect to wom-
      en, the Church and the poor.

      Chivalry rapidly evolves into the art of love, or fin’amor. This
      ideology aims to express the admiration for ladies. Indeed, wom-

    What is essential, my son, is that you show yourself to be
     such a man on both levels that you are both effective in
     this world and pleasing to God in every way.
       — Dhuoda, “Prologue”
  As soon as he is crowned, King Charlemagne expresses his
  military and political ambitions by the Latin term of renovatio
  regni (“restoration of the Roman Empire”). For the first time,
  a Frankish king campaigns not only to defend his territory, but
  sets out to conquer new lands. Throughout Charlemagne’s
  reign, fellow Christians and pagans both are subdued.
     Charlemagne sees it as his sacred mission to spread
  Christianity, so all conquered pagans and heathens must be con-
  verted — by the sword, if necessary. From his holy wars against
  the pagans grows the idea of the Crusades, in which knights can
  earn a place in Heaven by slaughtering as many unbelievers as
  they can.
  Paladins
  The most famous knights at Charlemagne’s court are called the
  Peers or Paladins. They are super-heroic knights on the path to
  sainthood. Many early Carolingian epics are closely related to
  hagiographic literature, as the ideals of the Crusade are present
  in many texts. The Christian knights fight the pagans, and this
  places these heroes on the same level as the God for whom they
  fight. Nearly all paladins finish their lives as saints.

      his book, the core rules for the Paladin game, is set-to

      year before Charlemagne’s father, King Pepin the Short,
  dies. The main information given here is narrowly set in that
  period, with armor and weapon choices, clothing styles, castle
  and horse types, and a general price list inspired by what we
  know of Dark Age Europe. Chapter 15: The Future, advances
  the chronology so that eleven game years emulate one hun-
  dred years of technological and cultural advancement through
  European history.
     Charlemagne’s reign lasts for 47 years—from the death of
  his father in 768 until his own death in 814. If you are starting
  to play in an ongoing campaign, be sure to check with your
  Gamemaster on the precise date.
  A  Paladin Chronology
  This chronology lists the crucial phases and events in the
  Paladin game. It can only hint at the richness of detail and
  variety to be found in the various epics and Carolingian sourc-
  es. Subsequent Paladin supplements will present these events
  in detail.

      Die-Rolling Conventions

      P
         aladin uses two types of dice to play: 20-sided and
         6-sided.
            d20: The abbreviation for a 20-sided die. If the rules
      say, “Roll 1d20,” they mean that the player rolls the die, and the
      number which is left face-up is the result.
        d6: The abbreviation for a 6-sided die. Usually more than
      one d6 are used at the same time. The abbreviation for multiples
      of the d6 is made by putting a number before the “d6,” in the
      form “xd6.” Thus, if the rules say “Roll 5d6,” the player rolls five
      6-sided dice and adds their results together.
        d3: This notation indicates that the player should roll a
      6-sided die, with results of ‘1’ or ‘2’ meaning 1, ‘3’ or ‘4’ meaning
      2, and ‘5’ or ‘6’ meaning 3.
        +N: This notation indicates that the player rolls all the
      dice appropriate to the prevailing situation, then adds a certain
      number (represented by N) to the result. For example, a typical
      starting character begins with 6d6+150 Glory, meaning he rolls
      6d6 and adds the sum to 150 to get his total starting Glory.
      Rounding  off Fractions

        When performing calculations in Paladin, round 0.5 and
      higher fractions upward and lesser fractions downward. For ex-
      ample, a character with a Damage value of 4.3 would have an
      effective value of 4, while a character with a Damage value of 4.5
      would have a 5.

      ways, such as in personal combat. Rather than merely saying “I
      win,” the Gamemaster sometimes requires you to make a d20
      roll against an appropriate statistic. For example, in combat, you

     If you describe your character’s actions in a very convinc-
  ing or creative fashion, you might not need to roll —in such a
  case, your ideas or tactics were well-conceived enough in the
  Gamemaster’s eyes to ensure automatic success.
     Your character may receive a “check” (short for “experi-
  ence check”). See Gaining Experience in Chapter 6 for more on
  checks and what they mean.
     The Gamemaster always decides if a roll is necessary or an
  experience check is warranted.
  Character  Statistics and Values

     The numbers on your character sheet are used to rate your
  character’s various statistics. Your character has six sets of statistics
  listed on the sheet: attributes, traits, passions, standings, skills, and
  combat skills. Spaces are also given for squire and horse statistics.
     Statistics have numerical values ranging from 5 to 21 for
  most characters in the game. What is a good value to have? In
  general, values around 10 are ordinary. Values over 15 are con-
  sidered superior, while values over 20 are heroic. Those lower
  than 5 are inferior. This is the range for humans; some monsters
  or magical characters have values of 30 or more in certain sta-
  tistics. A normal character’s Chaste trait might have a value of
  10. A paladin’s Sword skill might have a value of 25. An aged
  knight’s Strength attribute might have dwindled to 5.

        usage. Others remain in use, but have been trans-
  formed overtime to have a new meaning. Also, many game terms
  have specific meanings not carried by their common usage. Effort
  has been made to use these terms consistently, as given here.

title: Final Word
leftColumn:
Chapter 9 details the magic of the Paladin world, and how
      characters may benefit from prayer or be subject to the incanta-
      tions of sorcerers.
        Chapter 10 explains the Winter Phase — a time of the year
      when people take time to reflect on the past year. In Paladin, it
      is also when the character sheet is changed to reflect the adven-
      tures of the past year, and the ravages of time on the characters
      family and lands.
        Chapter 11 deals with the ambitions of knights, and the
      ideals they can strive to attain.
        Chapter 12 explains all you need to know about feudal eco-
      nomics, wealth, and markets where Player-knights may buy new
      equipment and sell surplus goods. The last section details some
      of the Carolingian treasures and enchanted objects.
        Chapter 13 deals extensively and anachronistically with the
      society of the Franks, presenting an overview of its power struc-
      tures, the royal court, the ways of knighthood and the facts of
      ordinary daily life, the essential precepts of the Frankish religion,
      and finally some necessary military information.
        The lands of the Franks are described in Chapter 14. It es-
      pecially focuses on Charlemagne’s future palace at Aachen, as
      well as on the duchy of Ardennes — the latter being the home-
      land for starting Player-knights.
        Gamemasters looking to further nourish their fertile inspi-
      ration may have a look into The Future in Chapter 15, where
      they will discover the unfolding of the Carolingian legends as
      described in the epics. The glorious fates of Charlemagne and
      his peers, as well as a whole range of secondary stories, provide as
      many sources for adventure. While reading through the detailed
      Frankish chronology, Gamemasters will find ample occasions to
      involve their Player-knights.
        Friends and foes are presented in Chapter 16, which fea-
      tures the most important non-player characters: Charlemagne
      himself, of course, and famous paladins like Roland, Oliver,
      Renaud of Montauban, and Ogier the Dane. An extensive list of
      minor characters completes the field of possible actors.
        Since the world is bigger than Frankland alone, foreigners
      and their strange ways are described in Chapter 17.
        Every knight needs opponents, and Chapter 18 gives you
      the stats for a variety of minor characters, from bandits and peas-
      ants to Byzantine Cataphracts. Animals, like horses, dogs and
      falcons, are a part of a noble’s daily life, but on his adventures a
